title: ABC Asks a Judge to Stop an Early Check of Its TV Licenses
summary:
TV stations need a license from the government to send out their shows over the air. A group called the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, gives out these licenses.

In April, FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr told eight ABC stations to apply to renew their licenses years early. The Associated Press says this came just after a joke by ABC host Jimmy Kimmel made President Donald Trump angry.

ABC and its owner, Disney, sued the FCC in August. ABC says the early check breaks the First Amendment, which protects free speech. It says it is being punished for shows the president does not like.

On Tuesday, ABC asked Judge Loren AliKhan to stop the review. A government lawyer said the case belongs in a different court. He said ABC's licenses are still valid.

The judge did not decide yet. A ruling is not expected until at least mid-October.
why_it_matters: Free speech rules protect the shows and news you watch from being punished just because a leader dislikes them.

background_read: TV stations send shows through the air using signals that belong to the public, so they need permission from the government.
The FCC is the government group that gives out this permission, called a license.
The First Amendment protects free speech, so the government is not supposed to punish people for what they say.
